By mapping these coordinates directly into the pretrained video model's native positional space, UniAction allows heterogeneous actions to condition a shared world model within the same spatiotemporal structure. We further introduce cardinality-calibrated attention to address the bias from differing action representation granularities. We evaluate UniAction on four representative action forms: force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose. UniAction outperforms conditioning alternatives in action following, and a single jointly trained model surpasses the action-specific experts, showing that heterogeneous action data benefit from unified model and joint training.

We quantify how non-Gaussian structure contributes to constraints on X-ray heating and warm dark matter from the 21cm forest using information geometry. We compare the power spectrum (PS), wavelet scattering transform (WST), and topological data analysis (TDA), and assess phase dependence with random-phase surrogates that preserve the full Fourier amplitude spectrum. Within this information-geometric framework, the Fisher matrix defines a local metric on the (f_X, m_WDM) parameter manifold, and changes in its volume density quantify the loss of local model distinguishability under phase randomization. For simulated z = 9 spectra with SKA1-Low thermal noise corresponding to a 1000 h observation of a 10 mJy source, WST gives the strongest individual constraints at the benchmark under the standard regularized estimator. Its native Fisher-volume density is about 3.6 times that of the PS, and the surrogate WST remains substantially more informative than the PS. At this benchmark, phase randomization reduces the WST density by about one fifth to one third, depending on the estimator, and the loss remains positive across most of the parameter grid. Second-order coefficients show a larger fractional loss than first-order coefficients. TDA shows a larger fractional loss at the benchmark but substantially weaker absolute constraints. Thus the phase-sensitive component of non-Gaussian structure contributes to local parameter inference, while most of the WST Fisher-volume density in the main noisy analysis is reproduced after phase randomization. The relative importance of phase-sensitive structure is distinct from the overall constraining power of a summary.

Masses inferred at different radii around one black hole can be compared to test the metric, but a disagreement between them can also be produced by matter between the probes. We ask when the two explanations can be separated, for static, spherically symmetric deformations $-g_{tt}=1-2M/r+\delta_n(M/r)^n$ with integer $n\geq 2$, working to first order in $\delta_n$ and in the matter. For probes whose inferred mass is rescaled by the local lapse, namely the shadow and the frequency of the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), we prove that concentric static thin shells of non-negative mass reproduce the inferred masses of a deformation if and only if its mass deficit relative to a distant anchor is non-negative, does not increase outward, and drops only where a shell can be placed. With a closed-form ISCO kernel, $-3(2n^2-n+1)/(2\cdot6^n)$, the shadow and the ISCO frequency exclude this shell class for $n\leq6$, and for every $n$ if the shells are confined to stable orbits. For the pair, the shell class implies the anchor-free inequality $M_{\rm sh}\leq M_{\rm ISCO}$, which a positive $n=2$ deformation violates by $\delta_2/8$ in $\ln M$. Excluding the shell class does not identify the deformation: when deformation and shells are fitted together, the data generally determine only an interval of $\delta_n$, and we state when it reduces to a point. We place these results in a linear-Gaussian description of multi-sector consistency tests that separates within-sector from between-sector information and splits the test statistic into components along and orthogonal to a deformation. For Sgr A*, where no ISCO measurement is available, the known disagreement between the Keck and GRAVITY stellar-orbit analyses gives a conditional significance of $3.5$–$7.1\sigma$ under our summary and covariance models, while its component along an $n=2$ deformation is at most $T_{\parallel}^2=0.19$, independently of the stellar response and of the response of the EHT calibration.

How much does city fuel economy vary across car manufacturers? Using the mpg dataset, we examine gas, front‑wheel‑drive compact, midsize, and subcompact cars from 1999–2008. We compare manufacturers while adjusting for engine size and model year, and we also account for the fact that each manufacturer offers several models. The key findings are: bigger engines get worse city mileage (intuitive), and once engine size is considered, transmission type and vehicle class have negligible effect. Even after adjusting for engine size and year, typical city mpg still differs by manufacturer by about ±6%, indicating that manufacturers have inherent differences in city fuel economy.

AI coding agents are increasingly used to explain and modernise legacy software, but it is rarely clear whether they read the code in front of them or lean on familiar cues. The Apollo Guidance Computer (AGC) flight software is a natural experiment: its Apollo 11 programs are among the most discussed code on the internet, yet they are written in a rare assembly language for a 15-bit ones’-complement machine. We build an executable benchmark from nine bit-exact AGC programs. Answers come only from the original assembler and a cycle-level simulator, and perturbed versions of the famous programs reassemble to byte-identical machine code. In a study of all 27 qualifying Apollo 11 routines, with an analysis plan fixed before data collection (two models, six setups, 189 behaviour items), we find three things. First, a simulator tool raised behaviour accuracy by 19 points for one model and 49 for the other, to 100% and 97%, and almost eliminated answers that matched an unmodified famous routine after a one-instruction change (6% to 17% of answers without it). Second, a structural knowledge graph served over MCP added no measurable accuracy beyond the agent’s own file search (difference −4 points, 95% CI [−22, 15]), though it lowered cost. Third, exhaustive grading on all 32,768 inputs showed that rewrites passing every sampled test still failed: at most 4 of 9 Python rewrites per setup were exactly right. Plain reading of pasted source was sensitive to names and comments for one of the two models. Benchmark, tools, prompts and all raw outputs will be released publicly.

We give a deterministic algorithm for exactly counting the satisfying assignments of an arbitrary k-CNF formula. For every fixed k ⩾ 2, on a formula with n variables and m clauses, our algorithm uses poly_k(n, m) space and runs in time (n + m)^{O_k(1)} 2^{n/(log n)^{1/2 + o(1)}}. Our algorithm refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), which postulates that deciding 3-SAT on n variables requires 2^{Ω(n)} time in the worst case.

Humanoid motion trackers reproduce diverse behaviors, but sharing a policy across bodies requires accounting for differences in structure, morphology and dynamics. We present MimicAll, a reinforcement-learning framework for shared whole-body motion tracking across heterogeneous humanoids. A structured embodiment descriptor is encoded into global and joint-aligned conditions, which are combined with observation history and body-matched motion references to predict joint-target offsets. Physics-consistent embodiment randomization, body-calibrated retargeting and heterogeneous simulation support training across 4,096 variants from 16 humanoid families. We introduce a benchmark of 464 bodies across five distribution strata to evaluate motion generalization, within-family embodiment shifts and unseen-family transfer. Controlled ablations show that embodiment information improves motion completion with simple concatenation, while self-attention yields the lowest global position errors. With equal training transitions, shared training achieves 99.4% 30-second success on randomized G1 bodies in 100STYLE, versus 42.9% for a single-body specialist. With Flat-MLP encoding and concatenation, continued training on a motion subset excluding obstacle categories achieves 98.3% and 93.5% 30-second success on 100STYLE for sampled training bodies and out-of-distribution variants within seen families, respectively. On an eight-motion LAFAN1 subset excluding ground and get-up sequences across 464 bodies, mismatched body conditions reduce self-attention's 30-second success from 61.7% to 47.0%, demonstrating a closed-loop benefit from embodiment information.

Robot policy evaluation informs deployment decisions and policy improvement, but physical testing and simulator preparation require substantial effort. World models offer a complementary route through closed-loop interaction in generated environments. Recent benchmarks have demonstrated their potential as policy evaluators through outcome-based evaluation (i.e., assessing task success or failure). However, such evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how policies fail. Misrepresenting failures can lead to incorrect diagnoses of policy weaknesses and make policies appear ready for deployment even when small scene changes cause them to fail. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure? To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three evaluation tasks. Failure reason tests whether models reproduce the observable errors policies make. Failure stage assesses whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution. Failure boundary examines whether models reproduce the conditions under which policies transition from success to failure under controlled scene changes in simulation. The benchmark covers manipulation tasks in the LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Experiments across seven world models reveal substantial gaps in their understanding of policy failures, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation.
